question.problem: If the speed of a rabbit is measured in $\text{in/min},$ what are the units of its acceleration?
question.worked_solution:
We can find the acceleration of an object by computing the slope of its speed-time graph. So, let's draw an example of a speed-time graph where the speed is measured in $\text{in/min}$ and the time is measured in $\text{min}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13945962/assets/ecdd2f132499a6be0c1d8fa48f021713e2019ed9e6660af041853f7e30766091.png)

In this case, the slope is computed as

$$
m=\frac{\text{change in speed}}{\text{change in time}},
$$

and so the units of the slope are as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{units of speed}}{\text{units of time}}=\frac{\text{in/min}}{\text{min}}=\frac{\text{in}}{\text{min}}\cdot \frac{1}{\text{min}}=\frac{\text{in}}{{\text{min}}^{2}}
$$

Therefore, the units of acceleration are $\frac{\text{in}}{{\text{min}}^{2}}.$

question.problem: A cyclist accelerates with constant acceleration from $0\,\text{m/s}$ to $20\,\text{m/s}$ in $10$ seconds. Find their acceleration.
question.worked_solution:
We can find the acceleration of an object by computing the slope of its speed-time graph.  To plot a speed-time graph, we need two points.

- The cyclist starts at a speed of $0\,\text{m/s}.$ This corresponds to the point $(0,0).$

- In $10$ seconds, the cyclist reaches a speed of $20\,\text{m/s}.$ This corresponds to the point $(10,20).$

Since the acceleration is constant, we plot the two points and draw a line through them as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13945962/assets/e60d9d6898bd8d49fb32860c439cb022c25850ff609b80ee486e71b48203b5fc.png)

The slope of the cyclist's speed-time graph gives its acceleration. The slope of this line is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{20\text{ m/s}-0\text{ m/s}}{10\text{ s}-0\text{ s}} \\  & =\frac{20\text{ m/s}}{10\text{ s}} \\  & =2\,\frac{\text{m}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the cyclist's acceleration is $2\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$

question.problem: A particle accelerates from rest with a constant acceleration of $1\,{\text{km/h}}^{2}$ for the first $3$ hours of its motion. It then travels at a constant speed for the next $3$ hours before accelerating with a constant acceleration of $0.5\,{\text{km/h}}^{2}$ for other $3$ hours. Which graph represents the described motion?
question.worked_solution:
We start the first line from the point $(0,0),$ since the particle starts from rest. Then, because the acceleration is $1\,{\text{km/h}}^{2},$ we draw a line with slope $1.$ 

However, because the particle is only accelerating for the first $3$ hours, we stop the line at $t=3.$ At this time, the particle's speed has increased by $1\cdot 3=3\,\text{km/h}.$ So, the first line segment goes from $(0,0)$ to $(3,3).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13945962/assets/7a9fd32e5705860064e597fcf9308fee457063e060d3adede260f109ca488201.png)

The particle then travels at a constant speed for the next $3$ hours. So, the speed remains at $3\,\text{km/h}$ for the next $3$ hours, until $t=3+3=6.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13945962/assets/e4c7e47150bf1c205c243c6fa1d0f0e24b7a69f27a8461791d495eb7487cf4f3.png)

After $t=3,$ the particle has an acceleration of $0.5\,{\text{km/h}}^{2},$ so the slope of the third line segment is $0.5.$ The third line segment stops after $3$ hours. To figure out the velocity at this moment, we need to find the equation for the third line segment.

Since the third line segment passes through the point $(6,3)$ and has a slope of $0.5,$ we can use point-slope form to write the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}v-{v}_{1} & =m(t-{t}_{1}) \\ v-3 & =0.5(t-6) \\ v-3 & =0.5t-3 \\ v & =0.5t\end{aligned}
$$

The third line segment stops when $t=6+3=9$ hours, and the velocity at this moment is

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =0.5t \\ v & =0.5(9) \\ v & =4.5\end{aligned}
$$

So, the third line segment stops at the point $(9,4.5).$ The final graph is
